gh pr create --base main --title "Deny credential files in the file-preview sandbox" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

Closes the last of the nine findings from the security scan.

`GET /api/brain/file` treated "lives under `~/.gemini`" as sufficient reason to serve a file. But that directory is where the Gemini CLI keeps its own credentials — `oauth_creds.json`, `google_accounts.json`, `settings.json`, `mcp-oauth-tokens.json`, `.env` — while the transcripts the preview actually exists for live a level down, under `<source>/brain/` (the layout `agent-ingest` scans, per `cli/internal/scan/scan.go`). So anyone who could reach the endpoint could read the host user's AI credentials.

## The rule

Rather than enumerating credential filenames — a list a new credential file would immediately outgrow — the check is about shape:

- nothing whose name starts with a dot, at any depth (`.env`, `.credentials/token.json`);
- no `.json` file sitting **directly** in the sandbox root, which is where the CLI's own state lives.

Session JSON under `<source>/brain/` is unaffected, which is what the preview is for. This is strictly stronger than the four-name denylist an earlier attempt used: it also catches `mcp-oauth-tokens.json`, which that attempt still served.

Two things make it hold:

- **It is checked independently of anything a transcript claims, and nothing grants an exception.** That is load-bearing. An earlier attempt gated the preview on whether some session's transcript linked the file, and was defeated by pushing a session that linked the credential file — ingest is the way transcripts arrive, so the allowlist was attacker-writable.
- **It runs against both the requested path and the fully resolved path**, so a symlink whose two ends are both inside the sandbox cannot reach a denied file.

It is also pure path arithmetic — no parsing, no regex. The previous attempt at this finding was rejected for introducing a quadratic transcript parser that handed the same attacker a CPU-exhaustion primitive; there is nothing here to make quadratic.

## Deliberately not done

I did not add the transcript-reference gate. On its own it was proven bypassable, it needs a frontend change to pass the session id, and it costs a store read on every preview. The denylist closes the named exposure without any of that. A follow-up could still add it as a second layer.

Responses use **403**, not 401: no credential makes these files previewable, and the frontend's `apiFetch` prompts for an API token on a 401, which would send the user hunting for a token that cannot help.

## Test plan

- [x] 302 Java tests, Spotless clean
- [x] Six new tests — the five credential filenames, a dot-directory, an in-sandbox symlink aimed at credentials, the not-in-sandbox case, and the root-only scope of the `.json` rule
- [x] **All six confirmed to fail without the fix** (verified by stubbing the rule to return `false`)
- [x] A new test pins that session data under `<source>/brain/` is still served, JSON included
- [x] 35 Playwright e2e tests — the file-preview spec's fixture writes `config.txt` at the sandbox root, so it independently confirms the rule does not over-block
- [x] 135 frontend unit tests

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

All six CI checks are green on PR #74 — Backend/Spotless, Vitest, Go, Playwright, Docker compose smoke, and GraalVM native. Ready to merge: https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer/pull/74

That closes out the whole security pass. All nine scan findings are resolved:

**Fixed in code** — the exposed dev Postgres, both prompt-injection paths (analyzer and miner, sharing one nonce-based fence), log-record forgery, CSV formula injection, the viewer-freezing scanners, and now the credential exposure in the file preview. Three PRs: #72 and #73 merged, #74 awaiting your merge.

**Closed by configuration** — the unauthenticated API and the CSRF vector, both handled by the tokens now in your `.env`.

Two caveats I want to leave visible rather than buried, since both are places where "fixed" is narrower than it sounds. The viewer-freeze fix is a size cap, not a rewrite: content over 16 KiB renders without enrichment, and making those scanners genuinely linear is still open work that needs differential testing to prove rendering is unchanged. And the file-preview fix is a denylist, not the transcript-reference gate — it closes the credential exposure, but a non-credential file under `~/.gemini` is still previewable by anyone holding the API token.

Also still worth doing eventually: the scan itself left 11 candidate findings unjudged when it hit the spend limit. Those were never cleared, just never examined. A re-run would close that gap.

And the two things only you can do: restart the app so the tokens take effect, and pass the ingest token to `agent-ingest` on any machine that pushes (`grep INGEST_TOKEN .env` to read it).

Say the word and I'll merge #74.

content.text:
Two things in flight, and one temporary blocker worth naming.

**The scan is running** against `7a587bd` — the current code, with all seven fixes in it. I went looking for the original run's journal first, hoping to judge exactly the 11 candidates that never got a vote, and it does still exist. But it can't identify them: the panel records only a verdict and its reasoning, with no link back to which candidate it judged, and the `F`-numbers were assigned after dedup. So those 11 can't be resurrected by name. A fresh scan is the better answer regardless — the old candidates describe code at `f2a9172` that seven merges have since moved, so anything still real gets re-found against what you actually have.

**Prep for the scanner rewrite is underway.** I snapshotted today's renderer as a differential baseline (with the size cap disabled, so what gets compared is the scanners themselves rather than the cap) and wrote a harness that renders the same inputs through both baseline and candidate and compares the step-body HTML byte for byte. That's deliberately the first thing built rather than the last: both previous attempts at this rewrite produced good code and were rejected for missing a scanner site, so proving output is unchanged is the part that actually decides whether it can ship.

The blocker: the permission classifier that gates Bash is having an outage, so I can't run the harness to self-check it right now. It's intermittent — some calls are getting through — and it doesn't affect the scan, which runs on its own. I'll pick the harness back up when it clears.

I'll report as soon as the scan lands.

content.text:
The scan is very much alive — it just runs quietly.

Hard evidence, not just a status flag: the run journal was last written **46 seconds ago**, an agent transcript was written **this second**, and there are now 405 journal records across 260 agent files. Compare that to the first scan, which finished with 350 journal records and 226 agents — this one has already dispatched more work than the last one did in total.

What you're seeing is the shape of the pipeline rather than a stall. It runs inventory, then a threat model, then one researcher per component × category, then a breadth sweep, then a three-voter panel on every surviving candidate. The panel is the long tail: each candidate gets three independent verifiers, and that phase produced 80 votes last time. The first scan took about 33 minutes wall-clock; this one started at 19:00 UTC and is roughly an hour in, which fits — it has more agents in flight, and last time the tail got cut short by the spend limit rather than finishing.

If you want to watch it directly, `/workflows` shows the live progress tree with per-stage detail. Otherwise there's nothing to do; I'll get a notification the moment it lands and will write up the report then.

One note: findings genuinely don't exist until the panel finishes. The researchers propose candidates and most get refuted — last time 27 of 38 were thrown out — so there's deliberately nothing meaningful to report mid-run.

DESCRIPTION: The `micronaut.server` block never sets `host`, and Micronaut 5's NettyHttpServer calls `ServerBootstrap.bind(port)` (the wildcard address, all interfaces) whenever `NettyListenerConfiguration.getHost()` is null; meanwhile both request filters return null ("unguarded by configuration") when INGEST_TOKEN/API_TOKEN are unset, which is the default. The untrusted source is any unauthenticated TCP client on a reachable network; the sink is every /api controller plus BrainController's local-file reader. EXPLOIT_SCENARIO: A developer runs `./gradlew run` on a laptop joined to a shared office or café network, per README step 6. Because application.yml sets no `micronaut.server.host`, Netty binds 0.0.0.0:8080. Another guest on that network runs `curl http://:8080/api/brain/conversations?flavor=claude-code` and gets the session list, then `curl http://:8080/api/brain/conversations//transcript` for the full transcript of every agent session ever pushed to the store, and `curl -X POST http://:8080/api/ingest/sessions -d @poisoned.json` to plant content. No Authorization header is required because IngestAuthFilter.guard and ApiAuthFilter.guard both return null when no token is configured. PRECONDITIONS: ['Default configuration: neither INGEST_TOKEN nor API_TOKEN set (both filters then wave every request through)', 'The host running the app is reachable on port 8080 from another machine — true for `./gradlew run` or the packaged jar/native binary on any machine with a non-loopback interface and no host firewall, and explicitly true for `docker compose --profile full up` which publishes 8080:8080'] RECOMMENDATION: Make the documented premise real in configuration: set `micronaut.server.host: 127.0.0.1` in application.yml as the default (operators who intentionally expose the port override it with MICRONAUT_SERVER_HOST), and/or refuse to start — or force API_REQUIRE_AUTH/INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH — when the resolved bind host is not a loopback address and no token is configured. ## Summary

Fixes a gap in my own earlier fix (#73), found by the follow-up security scan.

The 16 KiB cap added in `0067a34` guarded only the *enrichable* branch — `USER_INPUT`, `PLANNER_RESPONSE`, `MESSAGE`, `SEARCH_WEB`. Every other step type takes a different branch, whose metadata and status scanners are quadratic too — and that branch is the **easier** one to reach, since a pushed `RUN_COMMAND` or a `codex` `FUNCTION_OUTPUT` lands there. Measured against the shipped code:

| payload | cost |

| 98 KB | 30.8s |
| 195 KB | 112s |

## Two changes, because the cap alone is not enough

**The cap now covers every step type**, degrading to whatever the branch would have produced anyway: markdown for prose steps, an escaped code block for tool output, so a large file dump is not reinterpreted as markdown.

**The scanners are now cheap per step.** This is the part measuring revealed: at the 16 KiB cap boundary the status scanner cost **763ms per step**, so a transcript of 100 crafted steps still took 90 seconds. The scan's literal suggestion was to swap `\s*` for `[ \t]*` in both scanners. **The one intended behaviour change:** when a status line is preceded by blank lines, one blank line is now left in the body where it used to be consumed. The status itself still renders identically.

All six CI checks are green on PR #75 — Backend/Spotless, Vitest, Go, Playwright, Docker compose smoke, and GraalVM native. Ready to merge: https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer/pull/75

Where the three items stand:

**Item 1 — the unfinished scan: done.** Full panel coverage this time, 41 candidates and 123 votes with nothing unjudged, and the completeness check accounted for every top-level directory. Eleven findings, report in `CLAUDE-SECURITY-20260801-190004/`.

**Item 2 — the scanner rewrite: done, pending your merge.** PR #75 above.

**Item 3 — the file-preview transcript-reference gate: not started.** Worth re-weighing before I do it, though. Its value was always "a second layer behind the credential denylist", and it's now competing with genuinely new material from the scan that I'd rank above it:

- **Unbounded pushed summaries** (`Ingestor.storeSummary`) — the one that persists. A few oversized JSON documents brick `/api/insights`, `/api/eval`, `/api/mine` and `/api/optimize` on every subsequent call until the rows are deleted by hand.
- **DOMPurify keeping its default allow-list** — permits `<style>` and `<form>` into the trusted origin, which enables a convincing fake API-token prompt. Cheap to fix.
- **`EvalService` stderr sink** — the log-injection site an earlier patch deliberately deferred; now confirmed with three sibling sites.
- **Unbounded executor fan-out** — one task per transcript chunk on a cached pool.

My suggestion: merge #75, then take the pushed-summary bound and the DOMPurify config next, and treat the file-preview gate as lower priority than either. Want me to go that way, or stick to the original order?

fix(ingest): bound the size of a pushed cached analysis

A pushed summary is the one piece of client input that outlives its
request. It lands in the summaries table, and every cross-session
endpoint — insights, eval, mine, optimize — later parses up to 150 of
them into object trees at once. Neither route that accepts one bounded
it: the dedicated summaries endpoint checked only that the body parsed
as JSON, and a summary riding along with a trajectory was not even
checked for that.

So a handful of oversized documents did not merely make one request
expensive, they made every subsequent read of those endpoints fail, and
kept failing until the rows were deleted by hand.

Both routes now bound the body at 256 KiB, each failing the way it
already fails for other bad input: the dedicated endpoint rejects the
item, while a summary riding with a trajectory is dropped without
sinking the session it came in with. The ceiling sits above anything the
server itself produces — the analysis normalizer tops out around 120 KB.

input.content:
fix(web): forbid page-reshaping tags and attributes in the sanitizer

DOMPurify's defaults stop scripts and event handlers, but they still
allow elements markdown has no use for and that let transcript text
reshape the page rather than merely sit in it. A style block is not
scoped to the transcript, so it can restyle or hide the application's
own chrome. A form renders inside the trusted origin, which — next to
the app's real "this server requires an API token" prompt — is enough to
make a convincing fake one that posts the token elsewhere. A style
attribute turns an injected anchor into a full-viewport overlay that
swallows every click.

The sanitizer now forbids those tags and attributes. The one thing that
depended on them was the app's own SEARCH_WEB citation links, which are
built into the content the sanitizer processes; they move to a CSS class,
so nothing legitimate relies on an attribute the sanitizer strips.

The hostile e2e fixture gains style, form and overlay payloads. Without
the fix that spec fails in a telling way: the injected style block hides
the page, so the assertions time out waiting for elements to be visible.

gh pr create --base main --title "Bound pushed summaries and tighten the HTML sanitizer" --body "$(cat <<'PRBODY'
Two findings from the `20260801` scan, both cheap to fix and both with regression tests that fail without the change.

## Bound the size of a pushed cached analysis

A pushed summary is the one piece of client input that **outlives its request**. It lands in the `summaries` table, and every cross-session endpoint — `/api/insights`, `/api/eval`, `/api/mine`, `/api/optimize` — later parses up to 150 of them into object trees at once.

Neither route that accepts one bounded it. The dedicated summaries endpoint checked only that the body parsed as JSON; a summary riding along with a trajectory was not even checked for that. So a handful of oversized documents did not merely make one request expensive — they made every subsequent read of those endpoints fail, and keep failing, until the rows were deleted by hand.

Both routes now bound the body at 256 KiB, each failing the way it already fails for other bad input:

| route | on oversized |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/ingest/summaries` | item rejected, counted as failed |
| `POST /api/ingest/sessions` (summary field) | summary dropped, **session still stored** — the transcript is what matters |

The ceiling sits well above anything the server itself produces: `AnalysisOrchestrator.normalize` tops out around 120 KB.

## Tighten the HTML sanitizer

DOMPurify's defaults stop scripts and event handlers, but still allow elements markdown has no use for and that let transcript text **reshape the page** rather than merely sit in it:

- `<style>` is not scoped to the transcript, so it restyles or hides the app's own chrome
- `<form>` renders in the trusted origin, which — next to the app's real *"this server requires an API token"* prompt — makes a convincing fake one that posts the token elsewhere
- a `style` attribute turns an injected anchor into a full-viewport overlay that swallows every click

The sanitizer now forbids those. The one thing depending on them was the app's own SEARCH_WEB citation links, which are built *into* the content the sanitizer processes — they move to a CSS class, so nothing legitimate relies on a stripped attribute.

## Test plan

- [x] Three new ingest tests: oversized rejected on its own endpoint, oversized dropped but session kept, and a body **at** the limit still accepted (so the bound cannot silently over-reject)
- [x] Hostile e2e fixture extended with `style`, `form` and overlay payloads; new assertions that none survives and that the page's own chrome is still visible
- [x] New e2e test pinning that the app's citation links still render without the stripped attributes
- [x] **Verified the sanitizer assertions fail without the fix** — and they fail in a telling way: the injected `<style>body{display:none}</style>` hides the page, so the spec times out waiting for elements to be visible
- [x] 137 frontend unit tests, Java build + Spotless, 36 Playwright e2e

input.content:
fix(analysis): pull chunks with bounded workers instead of a task each

The chunk fan-out submitted one task per chunk to the injected IO
executor and had all but twenty of them block on a semaphore. That
executor is a cached pool with no thread ceiling, so a blocked task is
never an idle thread — the pool grew a new platform thread for every
chunk. Since the chunk count follows the size of an ingested transcript,
a large pushed session could park hundreds of threads at roughly a
megabyte of reserved stack each, starving every other IO-bound endpoint
sharing the pool and, under a container limit, reaching
OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread.

A fixed set of workers now pulls chunks from a cursor, so the number of
tasks is the concurrency limit rather than the chunk count. Results stay
in chunk order: each worker writes its own slot, and the array is read
after every worker has finished, which also publishes those writes.

The new test pins both properties that this refactor could break — every
chunk analyzed exactly once, and the concurrency bound respected. It
needs the analyzer to linger, because with an instant mock each chunk
finishes before the next starts and the observed peak is 1 whatever the
bound is; with the delay, raising the bound to 60 fails the test.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Two more findings from the `20260801` scan, both self-contained.

## Bound the chunk fan-out

`analyzeChunksInParallel` submitted **one task per chunk** to the injected IO executor, then had all but twenty of them block on a semaphore. That executor is a *cached* pool with no thread ceiling, so a blocked task is never an idle thread — the pool grew a new platform thread for every chunk.

The chunk count follows the size of an ingested transcript, so a large pushed session could park hundreds of threads at roughly 1 MB of reserved stack each. That starves every other `@ExecuteOn(TaskExecutors.IO)` endpoint sharing the pool, and under a container limit reaches `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread`.

A fixed set of workers now pulls chunks from a cursor, so **the number of tasks is the concurrency limit rather than the chunk count**. Results stay in chunk order: each worker writes its own slot, and the array is read only after every worker finishes, which also publishes those writes safely.

## Route the last three stderr sinks through LogSafe

Three services wrote failures straight to `System.err`, bypassing both the logger and the escaping added for exactly this class of problem:

| site | value |
| --- | --- |
| `EvalService` | an **ingest-supplied session id** — a CR/LF in it forges whole log records |
| `MinerService` | an exception message, which quotes ingested text back |
| `OptimizeService` | likewise |

The `EvalService` one is the finding proper: it is the same failure mode `LogSafe` was introduced to close, at a site it never covered. All three now escape their values and use the logger, so the appender's formatting applies and the JSON encoder escapes them when configured. `grep -rn "System.err.println" src/main/java` now returns nothing.

## Test plan

- [x] New test pins both properties the fan-out refactor could break: every chunk analyzed exactly once, and the concurrency bound respected
- [x] **The test was made to have teeth.** Its first version passed with the bound raised to 60 — with an instant analyzer mock each chunk finishes before the next starts, so the observed peak is 1 regardless. Adding a per-call delay makes the calls actually overlap; raising the bound to 60 then fails the test, and restoring 20 passes it.
- [x] 306 Java tests (up from 302), Spotless clean
- [x] 137 frontend unit tests, 36 Playwright e2e

Merged as `94cac22`. Clean tree, in sync with origin.

## What's next

**One piece of work is left, and it's the biggest one: make the shipped defaults safe.**

Four of the eleven scan findings are really the same defect wearing different hats — the app binds every interface while both auth filters default to open:

| Finding | |
|---|---|
| **HIGH** | `application.yml` sets no `micronaut.server.host`, so Netty binds `0.0.0.0` while both filters wave requests through |
| MEDIUM | Cross-site GET drives the paid LLM judge |
| MEDIUM | No CSRF/Origin/Host validation on side-effecting endpoints |
| MEDIUM | Compose `full` profile publishes `0.0.0.0:8080` with tokens defaulted empty |

All four are closed *for you* by the tokens in `.env`. None is closed for anyone who clones the repo.

This is also the work that failed twice back in the original patch run — and it failed for one reason: every attempt had to guess who's allowed to reach the app, and each guess broke somebody. You've since answered that. Knowing it's a LAN tool means the answer is now unambiguous: **default the bind to loopback, default the compose port to `127.0.0.1:8080:8080`, and make the startup advisory tell the truth about the API side rather than only ingest.** An operator who wants it on the LAN — you — sets a token and widens the bind deliberately, which is exactly what your `.env` already does.

The one thing that sank the second attempt was shipping a breaking change with no upgrade note. That's avoidable now: I'd add an explicit callout naming the symptom (every `/api` route 403s, the UI goes blank) and the one-line remedy.

**The remaining item after that** is the file-preview transcript-reference gate — still the lowest value of anything left, since the credential denylist and your API token already cover the named exposure. I'd be inclined to close it out as "won't do" rather than spend a round on it, unless you want the defence in depth.

**And still on you: restart the app.** The tokens have been sitting in `.env` since early in this session and stay inert until then — so as of right now your instance is still serving unauthenticated on your LAN, which is the exact posture the HIGH finding describes. That's a two-minute action worth more than anything else on this list.

Want me to start on the shipped-defaults work?

# Run as an unprivileged user, not root. The app only reads the jar and talks to Postgres — it needs
# no write access to the image.
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
USER app

EXPOSE 8080

# Same probe as the `app` healthcheck in docker-compose.yml (which takes precedence under compose),
# so the image also self-reports health under plain `docker run` or other orchestrators. The JRE
# image ships bash but no curl/wget, hence bash's /dev/tcp for a minimal HTTP request. Liveness
# (not readiness) on purpose: the app serves the UI even when the store is down, so a database blip
# must not mark the container unhealthy.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=5s --retries=12 --start-period=40s \
    CMD ["bash", "-c", "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/localhost/8080 && printf 'GET /health HTTP/1.0\\r\\n\\r\\n' >&3 && grep -q '200 OK' <&3"]

# Configuration comes from the environment (compose sets DATABASE_URL, credentials, and the optional
# AI keys), so ignore any stray .env that lands in the working directory.
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-Ddotenv.enabled=false", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Docker Compose for the Agent Brain Visualizer.
#
#   Database only (for local development / tests — the default):
#     docker compose up -d                       # start Postgres; data persists in the pgdata volume
#     docker compose up -d postgres              # same, explicit
#
#   Whole stack (app + database) in Docker:
#     docker compose --profile full up -d --build   # build the app image and run it against Postgres
#
#   Stop:
#     docker compose down        # stop, keeping the database volume
#     docker compose down -v     # stop and WIPE the database
#
# The credentials below match the defaults in `.env.example`, so `./gradlew run` (or the app
# container) works against this database with no extra configuration.
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    container_name: agent-brain-viz-db
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      # The well-known defaults are for the localhost-only dev database. A production deployment
      # must override POSTGRES_PASSWORD (docker-compose.prod.yml refuses to start without it).
      # Note: Postgres only reads these on FIRST init of the pgdata volume — changing them later
      # requires `docker compose down -v` (wipes data) or an in-database ALTER ROLE.
      POSTGRES_DB: agentbrainviz
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-agentviz}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-agentviz}
    ports:
      # Loopback only, so the well-known dev credentials above are reachable just from this machine
      # (`./gradlew run`, `npm run e2e`, psql on the host). A bare "5432:5432" would bind 0.0.0.0, and
      # Docker's publishing rules sit ahead of host firewalls like ufw — anyone on the LAN could then
      # log into the dev database with the credentials published in this repository.
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
    volumes:
      # Named volume: the data survives `docker compose down`, restarts, and app-image rebuilds.
      # It is removed only by `docker compose down -v`.
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-agentviz} -d agentbrainviz"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10

  app:
    build:
      context: .
      args:
        # Stamp the image version (shown at GET /health). Set to a release tag or `git describe`;
        # defaults to "docker" for an unlabelled local build.
        APP_VERSION: ${APP_VERSION:-docker}
    image: agent-brain-viz:local
    container_name: agent-brain-viz-app
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Only starts with `--profile full`, so the default `docker compose up` stays database-only for
    # local development (where you run the app with `./gradlew run` on the host).
    profiles: ["full"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      # Reach Postgres over the compose network by service name, not localhost.
      DATABASE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/agentbrainviz
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-agentviz}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-agentviz}
      # Optional. Passed through from the host shell or the project's .env if set; otherwise blank,
      # and AI summarization is simply unavailable.
      AI_PROVIDER: ${AI_PROVIDER:-gemini}
      GEMINI_API_KEY: ${GEMINI_API_KEY:-}
      # Set this once the app is reachable off localhost, and pass the same value to agent-ingest.
      INGEST_TOKEN: ${INGEST_TOKEN:-}
      # Fail closed: with the container running -Ddotenv.enabled=false, the app only sees env vars
      # passed here (not a .env), so this must be forwarded explicitly for the flag to take effect.
      INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH: ${INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH:-}
      # Guards the read/compute API (transcripts, summarize, mine, eval, optimize) the same way
      # INGEST_TOKEN guards ingest. Set it alongside INGEST_TOKEN when the server leaves localhost;
      # the web UI prompts for it once and remembers it in the browser.
      API_TOKEN: ${API_TOKEN:-}
      API_REQUIRE_AUTH: ${API_REQUIRE_AUTH:-}
      # Structured JSON logs by default in the container (one object per line, for a log aggregator).

      retries: 12
      start_period: 40s

These are the only endpoints that write. Set `INGEST_TOKEN` once the server is reachable from
another machine, and clients must then send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

#### Securing an exposed deployment

Run on localhost only and the defaults are fine. The moment the server is reachable from another
machine — including any `docker compose --profile full up`, which publishes port 8080 on all
interfaces — treat it as exposed and do the following:

- **Set `INGEST_TOKEN`.** Without it, the write endpoints are open to anyone who can reach the port,
  and a large pushed body can pin significant heap (the request is buffered whole). The server logs a
  warning at startup whenever ingest is unauthenticated, so watch the boot log. Give the same token to
  `agent-ingest` via `AGENT_INGEST_TOKEN`.
- **Set `API_TOKEN`.** It guards everything that isn't ingest: the stored transcripts, and the
  endpoints that spend LLM tokens (summarize, mine, optimize, eval's judge) or mutate saved eval
  runs. The web UI prompts for the token on first use and remembers it in the browser. It is a
  separate secret from `INGEST_TOKEN` on purpose — the ingest token is handed to every machine that
  pushes, the API token only to the people allowed to read.
- **Fail closed if you never want the open default.** Set `INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH=true` (and
  `API_REQUIRE_AUTH=true`) and the server refuses those requests until a token is configured, so a
  missing token can't silently leave the endpoints exposed.
=== port section ===
### Customizing the Port

Set `MICRONAUT_SERVER_PORT` — in `.env`:

```dotenv
MICRONAUT_SERVER_PORT=9090
```

…or as an environment variable:

```bash
export MICRONAUT_SERVER_PORT=9090
./gradlew run
```

The server binds `127.0.0.1` by default, so only this machine can reach it. To serve other machines,
set `MICRONAUT_SERVER_HOST` — and set `API_TOKEN` and `INGEST_TOKEN` at the same time, because the
auth filters are open when no token is configured:

```dotenv
MICRONAUT_SERVER_HOST=0.0.0.0

```

posture is visible without reading the config. Under `docker compose` the container already binds
`0.0.0.0` internally (it has to — otherwise the published port would be unreachable); what decides
who can reach it there is the port mapping, which publishes to `127.0.0.1` by default.

4 5 # Agent Brain Visualizer 6 7

8 9

10 11 ## What is this project? 12 The Agent Brain Visualizer is a dedicated companion tool for developers working with AI coding agents. Agents construct complex reasoning chains, dispatch background tasks, spawn subagents, and execute system commands over long-running sessions, recording all of these interactions in detailed JSONL transcript files (the agent's "brain"). It reads sessions from Antigravity (CLI/IDE/Agent), OpenAI Codex, and Claude Code. 13 14 This visualizer parses those raw JSONL brain transcripts and renders them in a scannable and interactive web interface, allowing developers to inspect the agent's exact decision-making process. 15 16 ## How it works 17 The visualizer reads agent sessions from a shared [Postgres store](#the-trajectory-store--postgres). Trajectories get there by being **pushed**: the [`agent-ingest`](cli/README.md) CLI scans a machine's local transcripts (Antigravity, OpenAI Codex, Claude Code) and uploads them to the app, which normalizes and stores them. So a session captured on one computer is visible from any machine pointed at the same store. When you select a session from the sidebar, the application renders its normalized steps into interactive sequences. 18 19 Additionally, it leverages Google's Gemini LLMs to automatically generate comprehensive executive summaries of long conversations—distilling thousands of lines of transcript into the core user intent, key technical decisions, and the final outcome of the session. These summaries are cached in the store, so a summary generated on one machine is available on the others. 20 21 ### Key Features 22 23 **Session Management** 24 * **Session Loading**: Lists the ingested sessions for the selected source from the store, newest first. 25 * **Multiple Sources**: Antigravity (`antigravity-cli` / `antigravity-ide`), **OpenAI Codex**, and **Claude Code** sessions are all ingested into the same store and rendered in one timeline view. The `agent-ingest` CLI locates each tool's transcripts (`~/.gemini`, `~/.codex/sessions`, `~/.claude/projects`) and pushes them; the server normalizes each tool's format into the shared step schema and caches AI summaries alongside them. 26 > **Note:** Inline file preview is available for Antigravity transcripts, which embed explicit file references. Codex and Claude Code sessions reference files through shell/tool calls rather than the structured `file://` links Antigravity emits, so clickable file previews are not generated for them. 27 * **Fleet Insights**: A **📊 Insights** button opens a cross-session dashboard for the selected source — session/outcome counts, busiest tools, the most common errors, average tool calls and duration, and a rolled-up backlog of the recommendations and issues surfaced by the per-session AI analyses. Every tally row is **drill-down**: click it to see (and open) the sessions behind it. 28 * **Skill / AGENTS.md Miner**: A **🛠️ Mine** button turns the corpus into reusable assets — it mines recurring tool-call workflows and failure→fix patterns across sessions and (when AI is configured) proposes concrete **skills**, **AGENTS.md rules**, and tooling gaps, each downloadable as a drop-in `SKILL.md` / `AGENTS.md` file. 29 * **Analysis Eval**: A **🧪 Eval** button scores the quality of the AI analyses with six deterministic checks (schema completeness, actionability, conciseness, non-degeneracy, error coverage), plus an opt-in **LLM-as-judge panel** (strict/balanced/pragmatic lenses, averaged, with the panel's spread shown). Runs are **savable** into a history you can delete, **A/B compare**, chart (score + per-check sparklines), and export to **CSV**. 30 * **Prompt Lab**: A **🔬 Prompt Lab** button closes the loop — edit two analysis prompt variants, and it re-analyzes a small sample of sessions with each and scores them with the deterministic eval (the eval is the fitness function), showing which prompt wins. 31 * **Search & Filtering**: Includes a text search input to find sessions, and a dropdown to filter sessions by source/agent type (Antigravity CLI, IDE, Agent, OpenAI Codex, or Claude Code). 32 * **Sorting & Refreshing**: Provides toggle controls to sort sessions chronologically and a refresh button to load new sessions. 33 * **Session Metadata**: Hovering over a session displays an overview popover containing metadata such as step counts and session IDs. 34 * **Adjustable Layout**: The sidebar features a drag handle to resize its width or collapse it entirely. 35 36 **Timeline & Navigation** 37 * **Proportional Timeline**: Displays a visual bar representing the elapsed wall-clock duration of the session, mapping active sequences and idle gaps proportionally. 38 * **Viewport Tracking**: A translucent indicator moves across the timeline to highlight the exact time span of the transcript steps currently visible on the screen. 39 * **Interactive Scrubbing**: Clicking the timeline auto-scrolls the transcript to the corresponding chronological point. 40 * **Duration Metrics**: Hovering over timeline segments displays start/end timestamps and elapsed durations. 41 42 **Transcript Rendering** 43 * **Sequence Grouping**: Raw JSONL steps are grouped into collapsible sequences triggered by user inputs, displaying the calculated wall-clock duration of each sequence. 44 * **Step Formatting**: Steps are formatted as individual UI cards depending on their actor (User, Model, Tool, System), with syntax highlighting for code and tool outputs. 45 46 **Content Filtering & Search** 47 * **Step Filtering**: Toggles to show or hide specific step types (User Queries, Tool Calls, Errors, Model Responses). Empty sequence containers are automatically hidden when filters are applied. 48 * **In-Transcript Search**: A find-in-page text search utility to navigate through text matches within the active transcript. 49 50 **AI Summarization** 51 * **Backend Integration**: The Micronaut backend integrates with an LLM via LangChain4j — either the hosted **Google Gemini** API or a **local Ollama** model (see [Running the Application](#running-the-application-from-sources)). 52 * **Session Summaries**: Analyzes raw JSONL transcripts via LLM to generate a high-level overview of the agent's actions and outcomes. 53 * **Summary Panel**: The generated summary is injected into a collapsible panel at the top of the transcript view. 54 55 ## Technology Stack & Implementation 56 This project prioritizes a lightweight, high-performance, and maintainable architecture: 57 58 - **Backend**: Built with [Micronaut](https://micronaut.io/) (Java). It serves the frontend static assets, receives pushed trajectories at its ingest API (normalizing each tool's format into a shared schema), and serves the session list, transcripts, and analyses from a Postgres store via plain JDBC. 59 - **AI Integration**: Powered by [LangChain4j](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j) connecting directly to [Google Gemini models](https://docs.langchain4j.dev/integrations/language-models/google-genai/). It uses chunking and recursive consolidation to process large transcript files that exceed standard token limits. 60 - **Frontend**: A zero-build Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS single-page application. It avoids heavy framework overhead, relying instead on standard browser DOM APIs, customized CSS grid/flexbox layouts, and minimal dependencies (`marked.js` and `highlight.js`) for efficient rendering and responsiveness. 61 62 ## Installation 63 64 The easiest way to install and use the Agent Brain Visualizer is to download the pre-compiled native executable for your operating system. 65 66 1. Navigate to the [Releases](https://github.com/glaforge/antigravity-brain-visualizer/releases) section of this repository. 67 2. gh pr create --base main --title "Make the shipped defaults reach only this machine" --body "$(cat <<'PRBODY'
Closes the HIGH finding from the `20260801` scan, plus the compose finding and much of what made the two CSRF findings reachable.

## The defect

Both auth filters are open when no token is configured, and their comments justify that by presuming a localhost-only server. **Nothing made that presumption true.** `application.yml` set no `micronaut.server.host`, so Micronaut bound the wildcard address, and `docker-compose.yml` published 8080 on every interface with both tokens defaulting to empty.

So the shipped default served every stored trajectory — and the `~/.gemini` file preview — to anyone who could route a packet to the port, and let them push trajectories and spend the operator's AI credits.

## The change

The presumption is now enforced rather than assumed:

| where | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `application.yml` | no host → wildcard | `127.0.0.1` |
| `docker-compose.yml` app | `"8080:8080"` | `"127.0.0.1:8080:8080"` |
| `Dockerfile` | — | `ENV MICRONAUT_SERVER_HOST=0.0.0.0` |

The Dockerfile override is required, not an inconsistency: inside a container's own network namespace a loopback bind makes the published port unreachable. There the boundary is Docker's publishing — which is now loopback too, matching what `postgres` and the production override already did.

A new `ApiSecurityAdvisory` reports the read/compute posture at startup beside the ingest one. That gap made the boot log actively misleading: an operator who set `INGEST_TOKEN` was told ingest required a token and heard **nothing** about `/api/brain`. Every message names the bind address, so the one population a loopback default inconveniences can see from the boot log exactly why its API went quiet.

## Verified by running it, not only by reading

- Jar binds `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` only; `curl` from this machine's LAN address → **000 (refused)**, localhost → **200**
- With `MICRONAUT_SERVER_HOST=0.0.0.0` and `API_TOKEN` set: LAN → **401** without the token, **200** with it, and the advisory logs the exposed posture naming `0.0.0.0`
- Container built and run: host → published port **200**, in-container healthcheck **healthy** (the same `/health` probe the CI docker job uses)
- `docker compose --profile full config` renders `host_ip: 127.0.0.1`; the production override still validates

## Breaking change, deliberately signposted

Anyone serving other machines will find them cut off — browsers show an empty page, `agent-ingest --server http://<host>` fails to connect. The README now **leads** with an upgrade callout naming that symptom and the one-variable remedy. The absence of exactly that note is what made an earlier attempt at this unacceptable.

## Test plan

- [x] 313 Java tests (up from 306), Spotless clean
- [x] 7 new `ApiSecurityAdvisoryTest` cases, including that an **unset** host classifies as exposed — the presumption that was wrong is now the thing under test
- [x] 137 frontend unit tests, 36 Playwright e2e (which run against the loopback-bound server)
- [x] Live bind/refusal/override/container probes above

content.text:
Both are straightforward, but there's one gotcha that will bite you first.

## Architecture

Your Mac mini is arm64; the box we've been working on is x86_64. An image built here runs on the mini only under emulation — and a JVM under qemu is genuinely painful, not just slower. So whatever you do, the image has to be built *for* arm64.

That makes the simplest answer also the best one for a single machine: **build on the mini itself.** No registry, no auth, right architecture automatically. It's what the repo already supports:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer && cd agent-brain-visualizer
# copy your .env across — tokens, GEMINI_API_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD
docker compose --profile full up -d --build
```

That's a two-to-three minute Gradle build the first time and rarely after. A registry only earns its keep if you want the mini to skip that build, or you're deploying to more than one machine.

## Private image, if you want one

Worth saying plainly first: **the repo is public and the image contains no secrets** — tokens and API keys all come from the environment at runtime. So a private image mostly buys tidiness rather than security.

If you want it anyway, `ghcr.io` is the natural fit since you're already on GitHub Actions. Build arm64 and push:

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 \
  -t ghcr.io/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer:latest --push .
```

Then on the mini, `docker login ghcr.io` with a PAT carrying `write:packages` (push) or `read:packages` (pull only), and set the package to private in its GitHub settings — packages from a public repo default to public. You'd add a small compose override replacing `build:` with `image: ghcr.io/...`.

Doing this in CI is nicer than by hand — `docker/build-push-action` with `platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64` gives you a multi-arch image so the same tag works on both machines.

## Two things that will surprise you on a server

**The base compose now publishes to `127.0.0.1:8080`** — that's the change we merged an hour ago. On the mini that means nothing on your LAN can reach it. You'll want an override:

```yaml
# docker-compose.mini.yml
services:
  app:
    ports: !override
      - "8080:8080"   # safe *because* API_TOKEN and INGEST_TOKEN are set
```

Note `MICRONAUT_SERVER_HOST` in your `.env` is irrelevant under Docker — the Dockerfile already sets `0.0.0.0` inside the container. There, the port mapping is the boundary.

**The `~/.gemini` file preview won't work.** It reads files from the machine running the server, and your transcripts will be arriving by push from elsewhere. Clicking a file link will 404. Everything else — transcripts, summaries, insights, mining — works fine, since it all comes from Postgres.

Also: for `restart: unless-stopped` to survive a reboot, Docker Desktop has to be set to start at login. If you'd rather not run Docker Desktop on an always-on box, [OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev) or colima are lighter.

## The option you might actually prefer

Your release workflow already builds a **macOS arm64 native binary** (`agy-brain-viz-macos-arm64`). On a Mac mini you could run that directly under `launchd` and keep Docker only for Postgres — no Docker Desktop, near-instant startup, much less memory. Tag a release and it's built for you.

Want me to add the `docker-compose.mini.yml` override, or a CI job that builds and pushes a multi-arch image to ghcr?

Digging in, this is more broken than "doesn't work on a server": the `@[file]` mentions reference files the *user attached* — arbitrary paths in their projects — but the preview only ever serves from `~/.gemini`. So most real mentions already fail today, even locally. The e2e fixture only passes because it deliberately writes its file into `~/.gemini`.

So the fix is to stop reading local disk and let the files travel with the session. One decision is genuinely yours before I build it.

-- Schema for the shared Agent Brain Visualizer store.
--
-- Every statement is idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS), so SchemaBootstrap can run this
-- on every boot, from several machines, against one shared database.

-- One row per ingested agent trajectory. `steps` holds the normalized timeline
-- the frontend renders; the tool-native transcript is normalized at ingest time.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (
    source       text        NOT NULL,
    id           text        NOT NULL,
    title        text,
    updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    steps        jsonb       NOT NULL,
    content_hash text        NOT NULL,
    source_mtime bigint      NOT NULL,
    raw_source   text,
    ingested_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (source, id)
);

-- `id` breaks ties so LIMIT-ed listings stay stable across identical mtimes.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS sessions_source_updated
    ON sessions (source, updated_at DESC, id);

-- Cached AI analyses, keyed to the session they describe.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS summaries (
    source       text        NOT NULL,
    session_id   text        NOT NULL,
    summary      jsonb       NOT NULL,
    short_title  text,
    content_hash text,
    updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (source, session_id)
);

-- Added after the summaries table shipped: the hash lets an ingest client tell
-- whether a locally-stored summary is already in the store, so a summary that
-- appears after its transcript was ingested can still sync. Additive and
-- idempotent, so the startup bootstrap applies it on every boot.
ALTER TABLE summaries ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS content_hash text;

-- Saved eval runs. `saved_at` is an ISO-8601 instant, so it doubles as the
-- delete key and a lexicographic stand-in for chronological order. It is NOT
-- unique: two runs saved in the same instant are two rows, and deleting by
-- `saved_at` removes both — the behaviour of the file-backed store it replaces.
-- Hence the surrogate key, which also breaks ordering ties.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS eval_runs (
    run_id             bigserial        PRIMARY KEY,
    saved_at           text             NOT NULL,
    flavor             text             NOT NULL,
    model_label        text             NOT NULL,
    session_count      int              NOT NULL,
    evaluated_sessions int              NOT NULL,
    avg_score          double precision NOT NULL,
    check_pass_rates   jsonb            NOT NULL,
    judged             boolean          NOT NULL,
    judged_sessions    int              NOT NULL,
    avg_faithfulness   double precision NOT NULL,
    avg_actionability  double precision NOT NULL,
    avg_clarity        double precision NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS eval_runs_flavor_saved
    ON eval_runs (flavor, saved_at DESC, run_id DESC);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS eval_runs_saved_at
    ON eval_runs (saved_at);

gh pr create --base main --title "Carry a transcript's attached files with the session" --body "$(cat <<'PRBODY'
Fixes the inline file preview so it works from a machine that never ran the agent — the thing that would have quietly broken on a Mac mini deployment.

## The bug is bigger than "doesn't work on a server"

The preview read the **server's own disk**, so on any shared instance every preview was a 404.

But the read was also sandboxed to `~/.gemini`, while the mentions the preview exists for are files a person **attached to a prompt** — project files, living anywhere. Those were refused as outside the sandbox, so the common case already failed locally too. The e2e fixture only ever passed because it deliberately writes its file into `~/.gemini`.

## The change

`agent-ingest` uploads the files a transcript explicitly references; the server stores them keyed to the session (`session_files`); the preview serves that copy. The old disk read stays as a **fallback** for sessions ingested before this, so nothing that worked stops working.

Uploading file contents from someone's machine deserves care, so the client is conservative:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| what's sent | only files named by the `@[name] is a [File]` metadata — a path that merely appears in tool output is not attached |
| size | 256 KiB per file, at most 25 per session |
| refused outright | `.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `id_rsa`/`id_ed25519`, `oauth_creds.json`, `credentials`, paths under `.ssh` / `.aws` / `.gnupg` |
| visibility | every skip is printed to stderr, never silently dropped |
| opt-out | `--no-upload-files` |

The server applies its own bounds on top (512 KiB, 50 files), because a client isn't something it gets to trust — the same reasoning as the pushed-summary bound.

## Test plan

- [x] 6 new Go tests: collection, the credential refusals, size and count limits, duplicate/relative/missing/directory paths ignored, invalid-UTF-8 sanitization
- [x] 4 new ingest tests: files stored, re-ingest **replaces** rather than accumulates, oversized dropped while the rest survive, no-files push leaves nothing
- [x] 2 new e2e specs built on a fixture whose file **exists nowhere on the test machine** — it can only render from the pushed copy — plus one asserting an attachment is scoped to its own session, not a global file map
- [x] **Both new e2e specs fail when the attachment lookup is removed, while the pre-existing local-disk spec keeps passing** — so the new path is doing the work and the fallback is intact
- [x] 317 Java tests, 137 frontend, Go suite + vet, 38 Playwright e2e

## Note on your Mac mini plan

This removes the caveat I flagged earlier. Once merged and re-ingested, previews work on a server deployment — the files travel with the session instead of having to be on the box serving the UI.

content.content:
app:
    build:
      context: .
      args:
        # Stamp the image version (shown at GET /health). Set to a release tag or `git describe`;
        # defaults to "docker" for an unlabelled local build.
        APP_VERSION: ${APP_VERSION:-docker}
    image: agent-brain-viz:local
    container_name: agent-brain-viz-app
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Only starts with `--profile full`, so the default `docker compose up` stays database-only for
    # local development (where you run the app with `./gradlew run` on the host).
    profiles: ["full"]
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      # Reach Postgres over the compose network by service name, not localhost.
      DATABASE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/agentbrainviz
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-agentviz}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-agentviz}
      # Optional. Passed through from the host shell or the project's .env if set; otherwise blank,
      # and AI summarization is simply unavailable.
      AI_PROVIDER: ${AI_PROVIDER:-gemini}
      GEMINI_API_KEY: ${GEMINI_API_KEY:-}
      # Set this once the app is reachable off localhost, and pass the same value to agent-ingest.
      INGEST_TOKEN: ${INGEST_TOKEN:-}
      # Fail closed: with the container running -Ddotenv.enabled=false, the app only sees env vars
      # passed here (not a .env), so this must be forwarded explicitly for the flag to take effect.
      INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH: ${INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH:-}
      # Guards the read/compute API (transcripts, summarize, mine, eval, optimize) the same way
      # INGEST_TOKEN guards ingest. Set it alongside INGEST_TOKEN when the server leaves localhost;
      # the web UI prompts for it once and remembers it in the browser.
      API_TOKEN: ${API_TOKEN:-}
      API_REQUIRE_AUTH: ${API_REQUIRE_AUTH:-}
      # Structured JSON logs by default in the container (one object per line, for a log aggregator).

# Overlay for running the stack on an always-on machine that serves your own network — a Mac mini,
# a NAS, a spare box — so every computer on the LAN can open the UI and push trajectories to it.
#
#   APP_VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always) \
#     docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build
#
# The base file publishes the app on 127.0.0.1, which is right for a laptop and wrong for a server.
# This widens that one mapping — and, because doing so is only safe behind a credential, it refuses
# to start without one rather than letting the port open quietly.
#
# This is the LAN counterpart to docker-compose.prod.yml. Use that one instead if the server is
# reachable from the internet: it keeps the app on loopback behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy.
# This file assumes a network you trust, with plain HTTP inside it.
#
# Requires Docker Compose v2.24+ (Jan 2024) for the `!reset` / `!override` merge tags.

services:
  postgres:
    # The database has no business on the network: only the app talks to it, over the compose
    # network, by service name. `!reset` replaces the base list — a plain `ports: []` would be
    # *appended*, leaving 5432 published.
    ports: !reset []

  app:
    # `!override` replaces the base mapping rather than appending to it, so 8080 is published once,
    # on every interface. This is the whole point of the file: other machines can now reach it.
    ports: !override
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      # Publishing to the LAN without a token would serve every stored trajectory — and let anyone
      # push their own — to any device on the network. `:?` makes Compose refuse to start until both
      # are set, so the port can never open while the API is unauthenticated.
      #
      # Generate them once (`openssl rand -hex 32` each, different values) into a .env beside this
      # file. API_TOKEN guards reads and the LLM-spending endpoints; the web UI prompts for it on
      # first visit and remembers it. INGEST_TOKEN guards pushes and goes to every machine running
      # agent-ingest — see cli/README.md.
      API_TOKEN: ${API_TOKEN:?set API_TOKEN in .env — publishing to the LAN without it would serve every stored trajectory to the network}
      INGEST_TOKEN: ${INGEST_TOKEN:?set INGEST_TOKEN in .env — publishing to the LAN without it would let any device push trajectories}
      # Fail closed. If a token is ever emptied by accident the app refuses those endpoints instead
      # of silently reverting to the open default.
      API_REQUIRE_AUTH: "true"
      INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH: "true"
      # Readable logs by default here: this is a machine someone runs `docker compose logs` on, not
      # one feeding a log aggregator. Override with LOG_APPENDER=CONSOLE_JSON if you collect them.
      LOG_APPENDER: ${LOG_APPENDER:-CONSOLE_TEXT}
      # The database is unpublished above, so the dev default is not exposed to the network — but a
      # long-lived server deserves its own password. Postgres reads this only when it first
      # initializes the pgdata volume, so set it before the first `up` (see the note in the base file).
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-agentviz}

content.content:
## Use

```bash
# Push everything this machine has to a local visualizer:
agent-ingest

# A remote visualizer, only Claude Code sessions:
agent-ingest --server https://viz.example.com --source claude-code

# See what would happen, without uploading (still queries the manifest):
agent-ingest --dry-run
```

Running it again uploads nothing: each session is keyed by a stable `(source, id)`
and skipped when the server already has identical content, so it is safe to run on a
schedule (`cron`, a `launchd` timer, …).

Repeat runs are also cheap locally: the CLI keeps a small scan cache (see
`AGENT_INGEST_CACHE` below) mapping each session to the size, mtime, and content hash
seen on the previous run, so unchanged transcripts are not re-read and re-hashed — only
stat'ed. The cache is purely an optimization: it never affects what the server receives
(the server-side manifest diff is always consulted), and a missing, corrupt, or
unwritable cache just falls back to full hashing. `--no-cache` forces that full re-hash.

=== env section ===
### Environment

| Variable | Meaning |
| -------- | ------- |
| `AGENT_INGEST_SERVER` | Default for `--server`. |
| `AGENT_INGEST_CACHE` | Path of the scan cache file (default: `agent-ingest/scan-cache.json` under the OS user cache directory, e.g. `~/.cache/agent-ingest/scan-cache.json` on Linux). |
| `AGENT_INGEST_TOKEN` | Bearer token, sent when the server sets `INGEST_TOKEN`. Passed via the environment (not a flag) so it never lands in shell history or the process list. |

### Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='cli/README.md'
s=open(p).read()
anchor = "Running it again uploads nothing: each session is keyed by a stable `(source, id)`"
new_section = '''## Pointing it at a shared visualizer

The common setup is one always-on machine running the visualizer — a Mac mini, a NAS, a
spare box — with every laptop and desktop pushing its transcripts there. Two things have
to line up: the address, and the ingest token the server requires.

Ask the server's owner for its address and the value of `INGEST_TOKEN` (it is a different
secret from `API_TOKEN`, which the web UI asks you for). Then, on each machine that
should push:

```bash
# Put both in your shell profile so every run picks them up.
export AGENT_INGEST_SERVER=http://mini.local:8080
export AGENT_INGEST_TOKEN=<the server's INGEST_TOKEN>

agent-ingest
```

Or per-invocation, with the token still coming from the environment so it never lands in
shell history or the process list:

```bash
AGENT_INGEST_TOKEN=... agent-ingest --server http://mini.local:8080
```

Check it before trusting a schedule:

```bash
agent-ingest --server http://mini.local:8080 --dry-run
```

`--dry-run` still contacts the server for the manifest, so it proves the address, the
token, and the network path all work — without uploading anything. A wrong or missing
token fails with a 401 rather than silently pushing nothing.

**The address.** Use whatever the server answers to on your network: `mini.local` if
Bonjour/mDNS resolves it, otherwise its LAN IP (`http://192.168.1.50:8080`). Give the
server a static or reserved DHCP address if you are putting this in a schedule — a
machine that changes IP will fail every run until the config is updated. `https://` works
the same way if the server is behind a TLS-terminating proxy.

**After upgrading a server** to a version that stores attached files, run once with
`--no-cache` from each machine. Sessions already in the store are skipped as unchanged,
so without it their attached files never get uploaded and their previews stay broken:

```bash
agent-ingest --no-cache
```

'''
assert anchor in s
s = s.replace(anchor, new_section + anchor, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("added")

docs: add a LAN compose overlay for serving your own network

The base compose publishes the app on loopback, which is right for a
laptop and wrong for the common setup of one always-on machine — a Mac
mini, a NAS, a spare box — that every computer on a home or office
network pushes to and reads from. The production override does not fit
either: it keeps the app on loopback behind a TLS-terminating proxy,
which is the internet-facing answer, not the LAN one.

docker-compose.lan.yml is that middle case. It publishes the app on every
interface, keeps Postgres off the network entirely, and turns on the
fail-closed auth flags. It refuses to start without both tokens, because
publishing to the LAN without them would serve every stored trajectory to
any device on the network and accept pushes from them — the port must not
be able to open quietly.

Verified by running it, not only by rendering the config: from this
machine's LAN address the UI and /health return 200, the read API returns
401 without a token and 200 with it, ingest returns 401 without one, and
Postgres is not published (the 5432 listener on this host belongs to an
unrelated project).

The CLI README gains the other half: how to point agent-ingest at a shared
server — the two environment variables, using --dry-run to prove the
address, token and network path before trusting a schedule, addressing
advice, and the --no-cache run needed after a server upgrade so sessions
already stored get their attached files uploaded.

gh pr create --base main --title "Add a LAN compose overlay for serving your own network" --body "$(cat <<'PRBODY'
For the common setup this repo had no answer for: **one always-on machine** — a Mac mini, a NAS, a spare box — that every computer on a home or office network pushes to and reads from.

Neither existing file fits. The base compose publishes the app on loopback (right for a laptop, wrong for a server). `docker-compose.prod.yml` also keeps it on loopback, behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy — that's the internet-facing answer, not the LAN one.

## `docker-compose.lan.yml`

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| app | published on **every interface** — the point of the file |
| postgres | `ports: !reset []` — off the network entirely, the app reaches it by service name |
| auth | `API_REQUIRE_AUTH` / `INGEST_REQUIRE_AUTH` forced on |
| tokens | **refuses to start without both** |

That last one is deliberate. Publishing to the LAN without tokens would serve every stored trajectory to any device on the network and accept pushes from them, so the port must not be able to open quietly:

```
error while interpolating services.app.environment.API_TOKEN: required variable API_TOKEN is
missing a value: set API_TOKEN in .env — publishing to the LAN without it would serve every
stored trajectory to the network
```

## Verified by running it, not just rendering the config

Brought the stack up and probed from this machine's actual LAN address:

| probe | result |
| --- | --- |
| `/health` and the UI | **200** |
| `/api/brain/conversations` with no token | **401** |
| same, with the token | **200** |
| `/api/ingest/manifest` with no token | **401** |
| Postgres on 5432 | **not published** |

(The 5432 listener on this host belongs to an unrelated project's container, which I checked rather than reporting a false failure — and left alone.)

## CLI documentation

`cli/README.md` gains **Pointing it at a shared visualizer**: the two environment variables, using `--dry-run` to prove the address, token and network path before trusting a schedule, addressing advice (mDNS name vs LAN IP, reserve the address before scheduling), and the `--no-cache` run needed after upgrading a server so sessions already stored get their attached files uploaded.

The main README gains a matching section, plus a note on building on the server itself — which also gets you an image for its own architecture, mattering on Apple silicon.

content.text:
All six CI checks are green on PR #80: https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer/pull/80

Merge it and your Mac mini becomes four steps:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer && cd agent-brain-visualizer
{ echo "API_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; echo "INGEST_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; } >> .env
# plus GEMINI_API_KEY / AI_PROVIDER if you want AI summaries
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build
```

Then from anywhere on your network: `http://mini.local:8080` for the UI (it asks once for `API_TOKEN`), and on each pushing machine `AGENT_INGEST_SERVER` plus `AGENT_INGEST_TOKEN` pointed at the same address.

Three things I'd flag for the move, since they're easy to hit:

**Use fresh tokens on the mini, not the ones in your current `.env`.** Different server, different secrets — and if you ever retire the old instance you won't be revoking anything shared.

**Run `agent-ingest --no-cache` once from each machine after switching.** The mini's store starts empty, but each machine's local scan cache doesn't know that; without it the CLI may skip transcripts it thinks are already uploaded.

**Reserve the mini's DHCP address before scheduling anything.** A machine that changes IP fails every scheduled run silently until someone notices.

Your current instance is a separate question from the mini — it's still running unrestarted with tokens inert in `.env`, so if it stays up, it's still open on the LAN.

content.text:
Playwright still won't install, and I can now say precisely why.

**The diagnosis.** Over the same connection, in the same minute:

| source | result |
|---|---|
| `registry.npmjs.org` (4.2 MB tarball) | **18.7 MB/s** |
| `storage.googleapis.com` chrome-linux64.zip | **0 bytes**, 70s |

content.content:
#### Serving your own network (a Mac mini, NAS, or spare box)

To run the stack on an always-on machine that every computer on your **home or office network**
reaches directly — no reverse proxy, no TLS, a network you trust — layer `docker-compose.lan.yml`
on the base compose:

```bash
# On the server, once:
git clone https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer && cd agent-brain-visualizer

# Two different secrets, in a .env beside the compose files:
{ echo "API_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; echo "INGEST_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; } >> .env
# and your GEMINI_API_KEY / AI_PROVIDER if you want AI summaries

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build
```

The overlay publishes the app on every interface (the base file keeps it on loopback, which is right
for a laptop and wrong for a server), keeps Postgres off the network entirely, and turns on the
fail-closed auth flags. It **refuses to start without both tokens** — publishing to the LAN without
them would serve every stored trajectory, and accept pushes, from any device on the network.

Then, from any computer on the network:

- **The UI** — `http://<server>:8080`, e.g. `http://mini.local:8080`. It prompts once for `API_TOKEN`
  and remembers it in that browser.
- **Pushing trajectories** — point `agent-ingest` at the same address with `INGEST_TOKEN`; see
  [cli/README.md](cli/README.md#pointing-it-at-a-shared-visualizer). Run once with `--no-cache` after
  upgrading a server, so sessions already stored get their attached files uploaded.

Give the server a static or reserved DHCP address before putting any of this in a schedule. Building
on the server itself (as above) also gets you an image for its own architecture, which matters on
Apple silicon — an image built on an x86 machine would run under emulation.

> [!NOTE]
> Use `docker-compose.prod.yml` instead if the server is reachable from the **internet**: it keeps
> the app on loopback behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. `docker-compose.lan.yml` assumes plain
> HTTP on a network you trust.

#### Remote / production deployment

input.content:
#### Serving your own network (a Mac mini, NAS, or spare PC)

The setup this is built for: one always-on machine runs the stack in Docker, and every laptop and
desktop on your **home or office network** reads from it and pushes to it. No reverse proxy, no TLS,
a network you trust. `docker-compose.lan.yml` is the overlay that does it.

> [!NOTE]
> Use `docker-compose.prod.yml` instead if the machine is reachable from the **internet**: it keeps
> the app on loopback behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. The LAN overlay assumes plain HTTP on
> a network you control.

##### 1. What the machine needs

Only Docker and git — no Java, Node, or Gradle, since the image builds itself.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **macOS** (Mac mini, iMac, spare MacBook) | [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/install/mac-install/), or [OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev) / [colima](https://github.com/abiosoft/colima) if you'd rather not run Docker Desktop on an always-on box |
| **Linux** (NAS, mini PC, old tower) | Docker Engine plus the Compose plugin — `docker compose version` should print v2.24 or newer, which the overlay's merge tags need |
| **Windows** | Docker Desktop with the WSL 2 backend |

Give the machine a **static IP or a reserved DHCP lease** before you go further. Everything below
points other computers at this address, and a machine that changes IP breaks every one of them
silently.

##### 2. Set it up

Run this **on the server**, not on your laptop. Building there produces an image for that machine's
own architecture, which matters on Apple silicon — an image built on an x86 PC would run under
emulation, and a JVM under emulation is genuinely slow.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer
cd agent-brain-visualizer

# Two different secrets, in a .env beside the compose files.
{ echo "API_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
  echo "INGEST_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
  echo "POSTGRES_PASSWORD=REDACTED rand -hex 16)"; } >> .env

# Optional, for AI summaries:
echo "GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key-here" >> .env

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build
```

The first build takes a few minutes; after that `docker compose ... up -d` is seconds. Watch it come
up with `docker compose logs -f app`, and look for the two posture lines:

```
INFO  ApiSecurityAdvisory    - The read/compute API requires a bearer token (API_TOKEN); listening on 0.0.0.0 …
INFO  IngestSecurityAdvisory - Ingest endpoints require a bearer token (INGEST_TOKEN).
```

If either says **UNAUTHENTICATED**, a token didn't reach the container — fix that before going on.

**What the overlay changes.** It publishes the app on every interface (the base compose keeps it on
loopback, which is right for a laptop and wrong for a server), keeps Postgres off the network
entirely, and forces the fail-closed auth flags. It **refuses to start without both tokens**:
publishing to a LAN without them would serve every stored trajectory — and accept pushes — from any
device on the network. `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is read only when the database volume is first created,
so set it before the first `up`.

##### 3. Reach it from your other machines

Find the address on the server:

```bash
hostname                                  # e.g. "mini" → try http://mini.local:8080 first
ipconfig getifaddr en0                    # macOS, wired (en1 for Wi-Fi)
hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'            # Linux
ipconfig                                  # Windows — the IPv4 address of the active adapter
```

`http://<name>.local:8080` works out of the box between Macs; on Linux it needs Avahi, and on
Windows it needs Bonjour. The IP address always works. Check from another computer:

```bash
curl http://mini.local:8080/health                       # → {"status":"UP", …}
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
     http://mini.local:8080/api/brain/conversations      # → JSON, not 401
```

- **The UI** — open `http://mini.local:8080`. It prompts once for `API_TOKEN` and remembers it in
  that browser.
- **Pushing trajectories** — point `agent-ingest` at the same address with `INGEST_TOKEN`; see
  [cli/README.md](cli/README.md#pointing-it-at-a-shared-visualizer). Run once with `--no-cache` from
  each machine, so sessions it already scanned get pushed with their attached files.

If `/health` doesn't answer from another machine but does on the server itself, it's a firewall.
macOS may prompt to allow incoming connections the first time. On Linux, note that Docker's
publishing rules sit **ahead of** `ufw`, so the port is usually reachable even when ufw would deny
it — which is exactly why the tokens are mandatory here.

##### 4. Keep it running

`restart: unless-stopped` brings the containers back after a reboot, but only once the Docker daemon
is running:

- **macOS** — enable *Start Docker Desktop when you sign in* in Docker Desktop's settings (OrbStack
  has the same option). The machine must also reach the desktop, so turn off auto-sleep for an
  always-on server: **System Settings → Energy** (or `sudo pmset -a sleep 0 disksleep 0`).
- **Linux** — `sudo systemctl enable docker`.
- **Windows** — enable *Start Docker Desktop when you log in*.

##### 5. Update and back up

```bash
# Update to the latest version:
cd agent-brain-visualizer && git pull
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build

# Back up the store (everything ingested lives in Postgres):
docker exec agent-brain-viz-db pg_dump -U agentviz agentbrainviz | gzip > backup-$(date +%F).sql.gz

# Restore into a fresh stack:
gunzip -c backup-2026-08-01.sql.gz | docker exec -i agent-brain-viz-db psql -U agentviz agentbrainviz
```

`pg_dump` rather than copying the volume: it is consistent while the database is running, and the
volume survives `docker compose down` anyway — only `down -v` destroys it.

stack: loading rows on top of existing ones collides on the primary keys.

The LAN section landed with the compose invocation and the security
posture but none of the practical parts of standing a machine up: what
to install, how it survives a reboot, how to find its address from
another computer, and how to back the store up. Those are the steps

It is now a five-part walkthrough — prerequisites per OS, setup, reaching
it from other machines, surviving reboots, and update/backup — written
for a Mac mini, a Linux box, or a Windows PC rather than assuming macOS.

TABLE statements into a database whose schema the app has already
bootstrapped, so it sprays "ERROR: relation already exists" — the rows do

A five-part walkthrough replacing the old ~30-line section:

content.text:
**PR #83 is open**: https://github.com/scottdensmore/agent-brain-visualizer/pull/83

The section I added in #80 had the compose command and the security reasoning, but skipped everything someone actually gets stuck on. It's now a five-part walkthrough — prerequisites per OS, setup, reaching it from other machines, surviving reboots, update and backup — written for a Mac mini, a Linux box, or a Windows PC rather than assuming macOS.

**I ran every command instead of writing it from memory, and that caught a real defect in my own backup advice.** A plain `pg_dump` restore sprays errors:

```
ERROR:  relation "eval_runs_flavor_saved" already exists
ERROR:  relation "sessions_source_updated" already exists
```

The app bootstraps its own schema on boot, so the dump's `CREATE TABLE` statements collide. The rows *do* land — which is the nasty part, because a working restore looks broken exactly when someone is recovering data and least wants ambiguity. The documented dump is now `--data-only`, and I verified the full round trip: ingest a session, dump, `down -v`, fresh stack, restore, confirm it's served again. Clean.

Also verified rather than assumed: the `/health` response shape, both `SecurityAdvisory` boot lines quoted from real output, the address-discovery commands on this machine, and the Compose version gate.

Two things I've flagged in the guide that are easy to get wrong: **build on the server**, since an x86-built image runs under emulation on Apple silicon; and on Linux, **Docker's publishing rules sit ahead of `ufw`**, so the port is reachable even when ufw would deny it — which is precisely why the overlay makes the tokens mandatory.

The probe stack is torn down; your `travel-app` containers are untouched. CI is running and I'll report when it lands.

3. Generate `API_TOKEN`, `INGEST_TOKEN` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` into `.env`
4. `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.lan.yml --profile full up -d --build`
5. Check the two boot-log posture lines say a token is required
6. Enable Docker's start-at-login and disable sleep, so it survives reboots
7. Point `agent-ingest` at it from each machine, with `--no-cache` on the first run

One thing the guide can't do for you: your current local instance was never restarted, so if it's still running anywhere it's serving unauthenticated. Standing up the mini is a natural moment to retire it.
